Esau and Jacob are twin brothers, the sons of Isaac and Rebekah, with Esau born first. Their relationship includes a significant exchange in which Esau sold his birthright to Jacob after Jacob demanded it, and Esau swore to the agreement. Jacob then gave Esau bread and lentil pottage. Esau later identified Jacob as the brother who had taken both his birthright and Isaac’s blessing.

Because of Isaac’s blessing to Jacob, Esau hated Jacob and planned to kill him. Jacob consequently feared that Esau would attack him and his household. Later, Jacob sent messengers to Esau, who came to meet him. The brothers reconciled by embracing, kissing, and weeping together. Esau offered to leave some of the people accompanying him with Jacob, but ultimately moved away with his wives, children, household, cattle, and possessions. Their separation was attributed to the abundance of their riches and livestock, which made it impossible for them to dwell together.

The relationship between Jacob and Laban began when Jacob fled to Laban after Rebekah warned him about Esau. Laban, Jacob’s maternal uncle, welcomed him into his household and hosted him for a month. Jacob then served Laban for agreed wages, particularly working as a shepherd and managing Laban’s livestock.

Jacob initially agreed to serve Laban for seven years in exchange for Rachel, and he subsequently agreed to serve additional years. In total, Jacob served Laban for twenty years: fourteen years for Laban’s two daughters and six years for Laban’s cattle. During this period, Laban repeatedly altered Jacob’s wages—described as happening ten times—and at one point placed a three-days’ journey between himself and Jacob while Jacob continued caring for the remainder of Laban’s flocks. Despite Laban’s efforts, God prevented him from harming Jacob.

Eventually, Jacob negotiated permission to leave with his family and possessions and departed while Laban was away. Jacob remained with Laban before sending messengers to Esau. Laban pursued Jacob, confronting him over the departure, the removal of his household possessions, and accusations arising from the search of Jacob’s camp. Jacob angrily challenged Laban over these accusations and over the hardships he had endured. The dispute ended when Laban proposed and established a covenant with Jacob as a witness between them.

Identified also as the LORD, God brings the Flood, remembers Noah, sends a wind over the earth, speaks to and blesses Noah and his sons, establishes a covenant, and promises never again to destroy all living things by such a catastrophe. God hears Hagar’s affliction, appears and speaks to Abraham, protects Sarah, enables Isaac’s birth, heals Abimelech’s household, and establishes covenants and promises concerning Abraham’s descendants. God instructs Abraham regarding the offering, is feared and obeyed by him, promises Isaac, blesses Ishmael, investigates the wrongdoing of Sodom and Gomorrah, and destroys the cities of the plain while rescuing Lot for Abraham’s sake.

God blesses Isaac with heavenly dew, earthly abundance, grain, and wine. As the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God hears prayers, observes affliction, enables conception, opens Rachel’s womb, and graciously gives Jacob children. God protects Jacob from Laban, blesses Laban for Jacob’s sake, alters the cattle’s breeding, appears to Laban in a dream, and serves as witness and judge. God directs Jacob to Bethel to dwell and build an altar, accompanies him with divine terror, answers him in distress, promises land and descendants, and commands his return to his ancestral land and kindred.

God is identified by Joseph as the authority against whom sexual wrongdoing is sin and as the source of dream interpretation. God reveals future events, provides Pharaoh’s answer through Joseph, establishes the prophesied outcomes, and raises Joseph to authority in Egypt to preserve life. Joseph fears and credits God for his circumstances, including forgetfulness and fruitfulness, while his brothers invoke God in recognizing revealed iniquity and questioning their returned money. God appears to Jacob in a nighttime vision as the God of Isaac, promises to accompany him into Egypt, gives Joseph his sons, feeds Jacob throughout his life, blesses his descendants, and remains with his family. Ultimately, God turns intended evil toward good, saves many people, visits Israel’s children, and fulfills the oath made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
